sample_answers.label: strong
sample_answers.text: The Python GIL is a mutex that protects access to Python objects, preventing multiple native threads from executing Python bytecodes at once. In CPU-bound tasks, multithreading doesn't yield true parallelism due to GIL contention; instead, I use multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor to spawn isolated processes with separate memory spaces. For I/O-bound tasks like network calls or database operations, I use asyncio where a single-threaded cooperative event loop context-switches when coroutines await I/O, giving high concurrency without thread overhead.

sample_answers.label: acceptable
sample_answers.text: The GIL is the Global Interpreter Lock in Python that allows only one thread to run at a time. So Python threads aren't really parallel. If you have heavy calculation, you should use multiprocessing, but for web requests asyncio or threading is fine because it releases the lock during I/O.

sample_answers.label: weak
sample_answers.text: Python is slow because of the GIL. To fix it you just use threads. Asyncio is basically the same as multithreading but newer syntax.

sample_answers.label: incomplete
sample_answers.text: I think it has something to do with thread locks and memory, but I usually just write normal async functions with FastAPI without thinking about the GIL.

sample_answers.label: strong
sample_answers.text: In our legal search engine, naive vector search failed on exact clause numbers and statutory codes. We solved this with a two-stage hybrid retrieval architecture: first stage runs parallel BM25 lexical search and dense cosine similarity using text-embedding-3-large with Qdrant, combined via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). The top 50 candidates are then re-ranked using a cross-encoder model (Cohere Rerank v3) to select the top 5 chunks. We also applied hierarchical parent-child chunking to preserve legal context without exceeding context token budgets.
